blocks.text: What an AI tool for UX research synthesis does

Synthesis turns raw research into findings. You read transcripts, tag moments, group the tags into themes and write down what those themes mean for the product. An AI tool for UX research synthesis helps with the sorting and the first draft. It does not decide which finding matters most to your team.

The useful jobs are narrow. Summarizing a long transcript, suggesting codes for one passage, grouping sticky notes that say the same thing and drafting a findings paragraph all fit. Judging whether a participant was bored or polite does not. A tool only has what you show it. If a moment was never written down or recorded, it is gone.

Think of the tool as a fast reader that only sees the pages you open. It can find every mention of refunds across many transcripts in a minute. It cannot tell you that a long pause meant the person was angry. That reading stays with you.
Where UX researchers spend their time

No public study we checked measures how UX researchers split their week by task. Email, docs, synthesis and scheduling are not counted separately. So the figures below are proxies from other groups of workers. Read them as signals, not as your numbers. UX research also has no category of its own in U.S. labor data. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts 952,700 market research analysts in 2025. That is a close match, but an imperfect one.

The clearest number for UX work comes from Dscout's 2021 survey of 300 UX practitioners. Analysis took the largest share of a recent project, at 32.7%. Recruitment came next at 26.6%. Delivery was the smallest phase at 6.7%. The sample was not random, and the study is from December 2021. Treat it as a signal, not a census.

The same survey found that 49.7% of respondents wished they had more time for analysis. The article gives 51.5% and 51.6% in other sections, so the exact figure depends on where you look. The direction holds in every section. Analysis is the phase people feel short on.

Microsoft's workplace data points the same way, though it covers office work in general. Its 2025 Work Trend Index says the average worker receives 117 emails a day. Most are skimmed in under 60 seconds. The same report counts 153 Teams messages on a weekday and 275 interruptions a day.

Its 2023 report adds a split. The average employee spends 57% of time communicating in meetings, email and chat. The other 43% goes to creating documents, spreadsheets and presentations. None of these figures is about UX researchers. They do suggest that messages will take a bite out of synthesis time.

How to synthesize user research on Mac with Lazur

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch of your Mac. It works in any app. Hold ⌥⌘, which is Option plus Command, to ask about anything on screen. It answers out loud. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

For synthesis, the transcript, Figma board or spreadsheet becomes the context. You ask one question about it. The answer comes back by voice, and Lazur can circle the item it means. You keep the typing and the decisions.

items: Open the transcripts or the board you want to code. Use participant codes instead of names.
Hold ⌥⌘ and ask for a first pass of codes on one passage. Check the codes against what the participant said.
Ask Lazur to group the notes that repeat the same problem. Have it read the groups aloud.
Ask for the exact passage behind each group. Open the source and confirm the words.
Rename the groups yourself. The label is the finding, and the call is yours.
Dictate or draft the write-up, then edit it before anyone else reads it.

blocks.text: The order matters. Ask for codes before themes. If you ask for themes first, the tool will smooth over details you still need. Keep one question per hold. Short questions are easier to check than long requests with several parts.
Worked example: coding a set of checkout interviews

Say you ran six interviews about checkout. You have the transcripts, a Figma board of sticky notes and a Google Sheet with tags. Nothing is coded yet. The first hour is reading. Lazur does not replace that reading. It helps you find the passages worth reading first.

Start with one transcript. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask what the participant says about paying. Lazur answers out loud and points at the lines it means. Read those lines in the transcript yourself. If the answer misses the point, ask again with the participant's own words. Do not accept a summary as a code.

Next, put your draft codes into the sheet. A dropdown list keeps tags spelled the same way across people. Our guide on [creating a dropdown list in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets) shows the steps. Then ask Lazur which codes appear in more than one transcript. Some codes will be noise. Remove them.

Then move to the board. Ask Lazur to point at the sticky notes that mention refunds. It circles the notes it can read. Count the circled notes yourself before you trust the cluster. A miscount here becomes a wrong claim later.

Last, write the finding. Keep the structure simple: what happened, who it happened to, how often you saw it and what the team should check. Dictate the rough version with fn. Then ask Lazur to draft a clean paragraph from your notes. Every quote in that paragraph must match the transcript word for word.
Prompts that help with theme-finding

items: What does this participant say about pricing? Point to the exact line.
Which of these notes describe the same problem? Group them and name each group in a few words.
List the codes that appear in more than one transcript. Mark any code that appears only once.
Where on this board are notes about trust? Circle them and read them out.
Draft two sentences on the refund problem. Use only the evidence on screen.

blocks.text: Good prompts ask for evidence and limits. Ask for the line, the participant code or the note's position on the board. Tell the tool to use only what is on screen. Those two habits cut down on invented claims. They do not remove the need to check.
Mistakes to avoid with AI synthesis

items: Accepting a summary as a finding. A summary is a starting point, not evidence.
Asking for themes before codes. The tool fills gaps with plausible patterns.
Trusting a quote you did not check. Paraphrases often slip into quotation marks.
Pasting names and contact details into a prompt when a participant code would do.
Letting one vivid participant set the theme. Count how many sessions raised the point.
Skipping the disconfirming cases. Ask what did not come up, and what the team expected to hear.
Writing the report from memory of the sessions. Re-read the transcripts that carry the claims.

blocks.text: The worst mistake is a quiet one. A tidy theme can feel right when it is only neat. Check each claim against the source before it goes into a deck. If you cannot point to the lines, the finding is not ready yet.
Checking AI output before it reaches stakeholders

Treat every AI answer as a draft from a fast, literal assistant. Run three checks before a claim leaves your desk. First, find the source line. Second, count how many sessions raised the point. Third, look for one session that disagrees with it.

Write the check into your report template. A short line under each finding works well. List the sessions that raised it, the sessions that did not, and where the quote lives. Stakeholders trust a finding more when they can see the count.

Keep a short note of what the tool suggested and what you changed. This helps when a colleague asks why a theme was renamed. It also shows you where the tool goes wrong on your kind of data, so you know where to look harder next time.
Edge cases: surveys, multilingual interviews and diary studies

Open-ended survey answers are where AI helps most with volume. A long list of verbatims can be grouped in one pass. Ask Lazur to cluster the answers on screen, then read a sample from each cluster. The tool sees only what you show it, so check that your sample is not just the first rows.

Multilingual interviews need care. If a transcript is in a language you do not read well, ask for a translation of one passage at a time. Check it with a colleague or a native speaker before a quote goes into a report. Translation drifts, and small drift can change a finding.

Diary studies and unmoderated tests produce messy, uneven entries. Ask for the entries that mention a specific task first. Then ask for the ones that do not. The gaps often show what people skipped, which matters as much as what they wrote.
Participant data and your employer's rules

Research recordings and transcripts often hold personal information. Your employer sets the rules for how you store, share and process that data. Follow them. Check your consent form and recording permission before you use any AI tool on a session. Ask your privacy or legal team if you are unsure whether AI tools are allowed on research data.

Lazur does not come with compliance certifications that cover your research data, and this page does not claim any. Here is what the product does. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

blocks.title: Strip names first
blocks.text: Before you hold ⌥⌘ over a transcript, replace names, employers and contact details with participant codes. Do this even if your policy allows AI tools. Less personal data on screen means less to protect.
Dictating findings and notes on Mac

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur turns your speech into clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That works in Notion, a Google Doc in Chrome, a Figma text box or a comment field. For researchers who think out loud after a session, it can save typing notes later.

Three features help with research notes. Snippets expand a short phrase into a longer block, so a participant code or a standard note header takes one word. The personal dictionary holds product names and jargon that speech tools often miss. Clipboard slots keep several pieces of text ready as you move between apps.

For a Notion synthesis page, a callout works well to mark a finding. Our guide on [adding a callout in Notion on Mac](/how-to/add-a-callout-in-notion) covers two methods. Dictate the finding into the callout, then edit the wording by hand.
Figma and Google Sheets for synthesis on Mac

Figma's desktop app for macOS needs macOS 12 or later, according to Figma's help center. The Mac build runs on Intel and Apple silicon. Figma's release notes list faster file transitions on desktop, dated May 1, 2026. Check your macOS version before you blame a slow file on the app.

For a clearer walk-through of boards, read our [Figma page for UX researchers](/for/ux-researchers/figma). It covers FigJam templates, voting sessions and memory fixes. For sheets, the [Google Sheets page for UX researchers](/for/ux-researchers/google-sheets) covers shortcuts, pivots and scoring.

Use Figma for the clustering and Google Sheets for the counting. Lazur helps in both by answering questions about what is on screen. It does not change the file for you. Keep the decisions in the board and the counts in the sheet, where the team can see them.
What Lazur does not do

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It is not a plugin or add-in for Figma, Google Sheets, Notion or any other app. It has no partnership with any app maker.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on the Mac. It is not a research repository. Keep study files in your research tool.

faq.question: Can Lazur do UX research synthesis on its own?
faq.answer: No. Lazur answers questions about what is on screen and drafts text when you ask. You bring the transcripts, decide the themes and check the quotes. Think of it as a second pair of eyes that talks back.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my research recordings to AI providers?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Check your employer's rules before you use it on participant data.

faq.question: Do I install Lazur inside Figma or Google Sheets?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a Mac app that works in any app. It is not a plugin or add-in for Figma, Google Sheets, Notion or any other app. It has no partnership with any of them.

faq.question: Which Mac do I need for Lazur and for Figma?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Figma's desktop app needs macOS 12 or later, according to Figma's help center. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Is Lazur a research repository?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a research repository, and it does not tag your library. Keep study files and tags in your research tool. Use Lazur to ask questions about the screen in front of you.

faq.question: Does Lazur click through my Figma board for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things and circles them. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

faq.question: How do I start with Lazur for synthesis?
faq.answer: Download Lazur for the Mac. The Pro trial starts when you first open the app and needs no credit card. Try one transcript before you move a whole study into it.
